This tutorial extends the SIR model of [A first model](simple.html) with age groups and contacts between them, compares two interventions, and fits the model to data.


## Age groups and contacts

Most respiratory infections spread differently between age groups. `stratify` splits each state by age: here into three groups, with the share of the population in each. `contacts()` says how much each group mixes with each other one: a contact matrix, in which row *i*, column *j* is the number of contacts a day that a person in group *i* has with people in group *j*. With contacts, β is the chance of infection per contact. This model also has an *outcome*, `cases`: the infections that are reported, here one in five.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
library(starsim)

states("S I R")
beta <- par(0.02, bounds = c(0.005, 0.1)) # A parameter that can be fitted, between these bounds

infection <- Transition(S, I, rate = beta * I)
sir <- Disease(
  infection = infection,
  recovery  = Transition(I, R, dur = days(10)),
  cases     = outcome(0.2 * infection), # One infection in five is reported
  init_prev = 0.0001,
  stratify  = list(age = list("0" = 0.3, "15" = 0.6, "65" = 0.1)) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+, with the share of people in each
)

matrix <- rbind(
  c(10, 6, 1),
  c( 3, 8, 1),
  c( 3, 6, 3)
)
make_sim <- function(...) {
  Sim(sir, networks = contacts(ages = c(0, 15, 65), matrix = matrix),
      total_pop = 1e6, start = "2025-01-01", stop = "2025-07-01", ...)
}
sim <- make_sim()
sim$run()
sim$results$sir$I$by("age")$plot()
```
<img src="advanced-age.png" alt="Infectious people by age group" />

Every state and transition has a result of the same name (`S`, `I`, `R`, `infection`, `recovery`), and so does each outcome (`cases`). `by("age")` splits a result by age group.

`make_sim()` makes a sim with these settings, plus any others it is given, so that every sim below uses the same ones: e.g. `make_sim(interventions = masks)`.


## Interventions

An intervention changes the course of the epidemic from some point on. Here are two: vaccinating 80% of people aged 65 and over on 1 February, with a vaccine that cuts their chance of infection by 90%, and masks, which cut transmission by 40% from the same day:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
vaccine <- vaccinate(efficacy = 0.9, where = sir$age >= 65, coverage = 0.8, at = "2025-02-01")
masks <- modify(sir$pars$beta, multiply = 0.6, start = "2025-02-01")
```

To compare them, make a sim for each scenario, and run them together with `parallel()`:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
scenarios <- list("No intervention" = NULL, "Vaccine" = vaccine, "Masks" = masks)
sims <- lapply(scenarios, function(intervention) make_sim(interventions = intervention))
msim <- parallel(sims)
msim$plot()
```
<img src="advanced-scenarios.png" alt="The three scenarios" />

`summary()` gives each result over the whole run for each scenario, as a data frame:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
s <- summary(msim)
s[s$result == "sir_infection", ]
```


## Data and fitting

A model is fitted by finding the values of its parameters that make its results match data. To try this where the right answer is known, make data from the model itself: run it with β = 0.025, and draw weekly counts of cases from it, with random noise as in real reporting. The noise is drawn with the true sim's own random seed (`rand_seed = 2`), since the noise in real data has nothing to do with the model's.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
truth <- make_sim(pars = list(beta = 0.025), rand_seed = 2)
truth$run()
data <- truth$to_data("cases", resample = "week")
head(data)
```

Data is matched to results by name: the column `cases` is compared with the result `cases`, and since the data is weekly, each row is compared with the total of the model's cases over its week. Data of your own can be any data frame with a `date` column and a column for each result. `sim$fit()` then fits every parameter that has bounds (here, β) to every result that has data:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
sim <- make_sim(data = data)
fit <- sim$fit()
fit$plot()
fit$pars$beta
#> [1] 0.02499076
```
<img src="advanced-fit.png" alt="The model before and after fitting, against the data" />

The plot shows the model's cases with the starting value of β (before) and the fitted one (after), against the data. The fitted β is close to the 0.025 the data was made with.

To see the uncertainty in the fitted model, run it many times as a stochastic model, as in [A first model](simple.html#many-runs):

```{r, eval=FALSE}
msim <- fit$sim$run(solver = "binomial", n_runs = 20)
msim$plot()
```
